title: Commander Focus: Whales, Banishing Knack, & H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship
content:
With a great number of modern Universes Beyond designs, there's a bit of a lag time that occurs between ones initial evaluation of the card, and actually considering its ramifications. A great many of these appeal to Melvin, perhaps annoyingly so, with characters like Seven of Nine, Unassimilated becoming a 7/9, or Shadowfax, Lord of Horses having Haste's reminder text called out. There's a knowing wink, a sensible chuckle, and then you move on with your day. To that end, a great deal of these newly-printed Commanders get lost in the shuffle following their debut, because these are largely surface-level jokes, or bits of trivia you might see on a shortform video interspersed with gambling ads. Very few of these have their true merits or horrors taken to their reasonable conclusion, and that's very much the case when we talk about the H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship.

This is a marvelous Spacecraft from the Star Trek main set, which does the adorable thing of searching for a Whale when it enters, and allowing for an extra turn by way of new syntax, once per game. For a great many people, there was the immediate shock of 'A Whale?', before writing off the obvious tutor target of Dreamtide Whale as being neat but not extraordinary. Those who've played Pauper in the last year, however, had a different reaction. 'A Whale'—followed by an exclamation mark—as we realized something absolutely horrible was newly-enabled. Yes, the subject of today is the occasional Pauper darling Steelfin Whale, but it's far from the only Whale we'll be aiming to spot as we go sightseeing. There's actually two very real combos, both in Monoblue, enabled largely by Whales, both taking center stage in this list. Let's dive below the surface, and talk about them.

"...search your library for a Whale card"

This line of text on a 5-mana Commander isn't a thrilling way to start, if we're being purely objective. Whales in Magic are few and far between (at least until Nauctis), but the good news is that average card quality on them is relatively high. Sure there are some stinkers like Killer Whale but compared to quite a few of the 'tutor a niche creature type' Commanders Whale is a pretty solid one to draw upon. Take for example, before we talk about the more relevant combo pieces, our humble Ethereal Forager. This is usually a ~2 mana flying 3/3 that gets back 1-2 Instants or Sorceries, and given we want to flex cards like Planar Incision to flicker and repeat the Bounty's tutor trigger, we can grab the Forager early on to continue searching through. Dreamtide Whale is also of course a slam dunk, nearly Stationing our Commander on its own, or fully so if we get its Proliferate trigger off. If we wanted to dig a bit deeper, there's also Horned Loch-Whale and its associated Adventure to shove attackers down the drain, or Aethertide Whale as a means of generating infinite Storm count off of infinite colored mana. It isn't pretty, but you can even dig through your Library with infinite colored mana, Waker of Waves, and another "Whale", Barkform Harvester. Simply discard and bottom the Waker over and over, filtering through two cards at a time. That's right—Whales can draw through your deck, so long as you have infinite mana, and a way to repeatedly tutor the Waker. How hard can that be?

Josh Brolin is in the driver's seat of our Commander, or something. Did anyone see this movie?

This does bring up an important point though, which is that Changelings are Whales; that's fairly obvious, but given Blue has seen quite a few solid options printed with the ability, it's a huge boon for the Bounty. Omni-Changeling is a clear pick, as having a Clone to find when applicable is just great to see, and as mentioned Barkform Harvester can help us reset key combo pieces or tutor targets, should they end up in the yard. The funniest Changeling we're keen to find, however, is one I've touched on already in another Commander Focus with a typal subtheme: Orvar, the All-Form. Yes, Monoblue's fourth-most-popular Commander is a Whale, and given our density of blink effects he's often just a way to find more Whales, as we repeat the Enters trigger on the Bounty. Beyond Blinks however, one of the deck's essential combo pieces (both of them, even) are single-target Instants, which mean we get additional knock-on synergy beyond the blinks and protection spells we're already running.

The cards in question are a pair you've likely seen if you've played any competitive format, being Banishing Knack & Retraction Helix. These cards have a long history of going infinite, whether with Jeskai Ascendancy in Modern, Rona, Herald of Invasion/Valley Floodcaller in Pioneer, or our target, Pauper darling Steelfin Whale. The effect these Instants give to any untap-happy Creature allows them to go infinite in any number of ways, usually via a mana-positive rock such as Sol Ring, a Moxen, or even something like a Monolith. Moreover, even if we take these cards at their fairest, it probably results in bouncing every nonland our opponents control, so in a pinch they're like a build-your-own Cyclonic Rift. Not bad for a 1-mana Orvar trigger.

Station to Station

The Thin White Duke referred to a Beluga, presumably.

Steelfin Whale specifically is a rather interesting card for the Bounty, because while it of course does silly things with a Knack effect, it also just Stations up cards extremely well. This matters for the Bounty of course, but we're on more than a few ways to make use of the ample power behind some of our cetacean comrades. With this deck having quite a high density of Artifacts, we can use things like Steelfin or Dreamtide to turbo out the full effect of Uthros, Titanic Godcore, which in turn helps us go mana-positive on another very specific whale. This can also help enable the full might of what is likely the best pre-Star Trek Spacecraft, Uthros Research Craft. Once this is big enough, it's not only a draw engine and threatening attacker, but also big enough to Station our Commander, or load up the final main Station target, Queen's Diamond. Queen's Diamond is a card that seems absolutely insane in any deck that can take advantage of its restricted mana, the likes of which have either a Commander they expect to die over and over again, or be targeted down by the table. I wouldn't call the H.M.S. Bounty a 'kill-on-sight' Commander, but it does quite enjoy being sacrificed and recast to tutor once more. As mentioned, so long as we have infinite mana and infinite means of making the Bounty re-enter, we can draw through the deck via Waker & Barkform...and a great way of getting there can be making Omni-Changeling into a copy of our Commander, and recasting the original infinitely, putting it back in the Command Zone due to the Legend Rule each time. The conditions to allow for this seem asinine, but let me remind you, basically everything but the mana engine are Whales.

On the topic of Stationing however, I'd like to bring up something we aren't doing, which is abusing Luxior, Giada's Gift. In a more fair version of this list, we can effectively turn the Charge counters placed on our Commander into +1/+1 counters, leading to fairly quick kills with Commander Damage, especially if we've yet to take an Extra Turn that game. Funneling ~18 power worth of Station into the Bounty isn't very difficult, but it is a fairly fragile gameplan, and tends to be antithetical to our normal path of blinking the ship. I say all of this because—if you wanted a more fair version of the deck, for whom lower-power tables would be an option—that's an excellent path to go down. That's true of frankly any Spacecraft Commander, and something to keep in mind as the subtype proliferates throughout the format. This can be said as well for Genji Glove, which provides an extra combat on top of Double Strike, leading to a whopping 3 additional turns. These aren't especially safe bets though, and it can often be preferable to keep the Bounty or the Research Craft as noncreatures for as long as one can, because it allows you to better dodge board wipes. Knowing when you want to attack with the Bounty, or not, determines the accessibility of certain combo lines later in the game. This is because of the oddity that is Bounty's single use-ish Extra Turn.

Turn, Turn, Turn

Before touching upon the win conditions in detail, I first want to broach the topic of Extra Turns with the Bounty, because its trigger is fairly novel and we've not gone into detail on it thus far. When it connects with an opponent, you always draw a card, then if you haven't taken an Extra Turn that game, and control a Whale, a delayed trigger is created to take an Extra Turn. Notably, the actual turn occurring is not contingent on having taken no Extra Turns, only the initial trigger; therefore if you copy the trigger or cause it to trigger again, on a turn wherein you've not taken Extra Turns previously, you can take as many as you like. Of course if you're already taking infinite (or close enough) triggers or Extra Combats, the spare turns are putting a hat on a hat. This is doubly true in Bracket 3, where chaining turns together is forbidden by writ of the Bracket, so we're on just a single way to copy this trigger, being Peter Parker's Camera. There's a world where you could play & copy something like a Vantress Visions via Virtue of Knowledge, but I'm of the opinion that less is more, in terms of the Bounty's combat trigger. The more important thing it's actually doing is closer to simply being a once-per-game Haste enabler, if we really boil it down to how the turn gets used. Oftentimes, in order to secure the necessary pieces for our win, we'll either need to have a Steelfin Whale without summoning sickness, and/or get back a Knack effect via Ethereal Forager. Ultimately, you can just flex your first tutor as Dreamtide, Station up the ship + Proliferate, and treat its effect as a boneless Explore—a draw+Land drop. That's fine if you don't want to think about holding your turn as part of a combo.

There's one Whale in here we've not yet talked about, and it's the oldest one to see inclusion. I'm talking about boneless Palinchron itself, Great Whale. For a long time this was the 'budget' version played for redundancy alongside Peregrine Drake, but given its reserve list status it's crept up in spite of being worse than its contemporaries. The thing is, neither of those contemporaries were Whales. By way of either Orvar or Displacer Kitten, we can use Mind Games to generate infinite mana in most scenarios, via untapping our Lands repeatedly with additional copies or flickers. Mind Games as a card is especially cool as an enabler for this, because it can be found through the exact same pieces that we use to grab Knack effects, also being a 1-mana Blue Instant. Micromancer, Spellseeker, even Dizzy Spell can all either grab either a targeting, Buyback-able piece or Knack, depending on which is more advantageous. The largest factor determining which endgame you'll be shooting for is your available mana—Great Whale certainly has a higher ceiling, but requires you start things off by casting a 7-drop, to say nothing of Orvar, & Mind Games. Usually the Steelfin combo is available with 2-3 mana, due to Affinity and the nature of its combo pieces being either free or mana-positive. If you're strapped for resources, the latter is less plug-and-play (as it often generates colorless mana) but far more accessible at minimal mana. Do note it requires access to Haste and/or a turn, however.

They call it Knack II because there's two copies of the effect.

Just to make it clear, given these combos vary in their degree of esotericism:

  • Combo 1 requires a hasty/non-sick Steelfin Whale, any 0-mana Artifact/Artifact which goes mana positive e.g. Mana Vault, & a Knack effect (Banishing Knack/Retraction Helix). Target the Whale, bounce your Artifact, play it again to untap the Whale, rinse and repeat for infinite storm count/Artifacts entering/Blue Creature tapping/etc. Once infinite mana is achieved, repeat targeting the Bounty, to infinitely tutor Whales and dig through deck via Waker of Waves you reset to Library with Barkform Harvester. Finish with Brain Freeze->Faerie Mastermind activation.
  • Combo 2 requires Orvar/Displacer Kitten, Great Whale, & Mind Games. Cast and/or target your Whale with the Mind Games, either flickering it or copying it. Rinse and repeat for infinite mana if you have Lands which produce >4 mana, which can then be funneled into copying/flickering the Bounty for infinite tutors into the same endgame as Combo 1.
  • If for some reason you cannot bounce and/or flicker your Bounty, you can search for Omni-Changeling to become a copy of it, and infinitely cast & have it die to the Legend Rule. This can be paid for via Queen's Diamond, which in turn can be fed Station power via the copied/blinked Great Whale. Note also that any endgame with Brain Freeze->Faerie Mastermind can do just fine with one of the two, as we can stack infinite Mastermind draws with Barkform Harvester activations, thereby ensuring we always have a card to draw from bottom. Similarly, Brain Freeze and just waiting for opponents to draw is also fine, if all you have from your combo is infinite Storm count.
  • Finally, remember that Ethereal Forager can be used alongside a Haste enabler and/or Extra Turn in order to try again on a failed combo, or recur pieces which have gone to the yard. If for some reason you cannot Brain Freeze/loop Waker, Mastermind activations with cards in your yard can draw out opponents while Barkform Harvester is continuously shuffling back your pieces. For this reason, the Barkform/Waker package is the most important thing to not see exiled, as between the two you can 'fix' any issues that crop up outside of a Rest in Peace.

A Whale-Oiled Machine

Beyond Whales, combo pieces, & tutors, you don't have much in the 99. This is a shockingly trim list for how esoteric some of its core pieces are; your mana rocks all get to be mana-positive combo pieces we can use for Steelfin, our flicker pieces to reset our Commander are functionally tutors (and often protection), and things that would normally be cantrips get to be Whales, e.g. Waker of Waves as a 2 mana Consider. In terms of our ramp which isn't mana rocks that go positive, there's pieces like Renowned Weaponsmith & Vedalken Engineer, which each help us push for a turn 3 Bounty, on top of translating their mana into unrestricted resources by way of the untap ability on Grim Monolith & Basalt Monolith. Bilbo, Thief in the Night functionally reduces the cost of our Commander, and can re-up a blink from the yard to act as...another tutor. For a while, we even had Universal Automaton in here as a Whale for {1}, which would become {0} by virtue of either Etherium Sculptor or Shuri, Wakandan Inventor. That ended up being a bit unnecessary, as we really didn't want to play a true vanilla even if it could serve as a combo piece—far better was it to just make sure we mulliganed, Tezzeret-ed, or otherwise tutored something like a Sol Ring at some point.

The final few slots belong to non-Whale card advantage, and some odd ramp pieces. First and foremost, there's obviously Rhystic Study as the final Game Changer here (the other two being mana-positive rocks). This is supplemented with a Mirrormade, which can either be our Commander or another Rhystic, or even something like a Sol Ring. Faerie Mastermind is a great advantage engine, and even helps us ensure a win by way of Brain Freeze via its ability to force card draw around the table. New to the game, however, is Nyota Uhura, Communications, and I'm quite high on her! Talion on 2 does fantastic work, and coming down at one fewer mana really does a ton, even if you lack the life loss component. As for mana, Energy Tap makes great use of the fact a lot of our Whales cost a ton, with special mention to Ethereal Forager's 6-for-2 thanks to Delve. Dream Halls meanwhile exists to expedite our Great Whale lines, as nobody has time for the full 7 cost in this day and age. We can readily find and pitch spare Creatures thanks to, say it with me, our Commander's capacity to tutor Whales.

Example Decklist: H.M.S. Bounty, Steelfin Speedrunner

While we aren't a dedicated Proliferate strategy, the fact we often tutor Dreamtide fairly early does mean it's worth building around a few counter synergies. These are largely in the small-scale, such as duplicating the Shield counter from Diamond City or retaining Saprazzan Skerry for longer than expected. Two fantastic use cases exist however that put some real threat behind Dreamtide Whale being allowed to survive, namely The Theorist, Jace Beleren & Lost in the Maze. The Theorist is like a boneless The One Ring, but comes attached to some solid removal. If we're able to plus him enough to use it twice in a row, expensive Commanders just...aren't allowed to exist. Much the same can be said of Lost in Maze, whose Stun counters can be a real pain to handle, on top of the universal Hexproof access thanks to having several Station-able permanents at all points in the game. Speaking of tapping, Unctus, Grand Metatect is an absolute stand-out here, giving our Steelfin the ability to loot...although frankly, given Station we can bet on abusing the hell out of that ability boardwide. One last funny interaction is via Shuri, who can turn one of your other Artifacts into a Bounty on the turn you swing to get an Extra Turn...thereby getting you another one. It doesn't come up much (and hasn't, in testing) but when it does I'm ready to squeal in delight.

One last thing, regarding "Whales"—that is to say, Changelings. We're playing three, between Orvar, Barkform, & Omni-, and because we can find them readily it is within our best interest to run some off-typal synergies which are low enough in opportunity cost to be okay without controlling their respective type. Most notable among these is Mana Sculpt, a spell that kind of died on arrival from Secrets of Strixhaven, which is essentially Mana Drain's little brother. We have a vested interest in bulk Colorless mana, so while I'm normally bearish on Counterspells which cost 2 or more, these end up worthwhile most of the time. Think of them like slow rituals we can save our ass with. Beyond that, Trenzalore Clocktower comes up fairly frequently, as between Dreamtide and our endpoint combo untapping Lands infinitely, in the case of Great Whale, we can flex it as a bona fide Timetwist because a few of our Whales are Time Lords.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

I've actually taken the liberty of reducing this list's power from where it stood in earlier versions, by taking away both Rings of Brighthearth & Power Artifact. Each of these goes infinite with one or both of our Monoliths, and makes for an extremely concise combo by which we can accrue infinite mana. I want to be doing so via Whales, and as such simply included more tutors to compensate; if you wanted to power up the Bounty, being able to play more Game Changers (given we can't even afford a Cyc Rift or TOR, with all three slots being spoken-for) is a huge buff. Powering down is likewise fairly easy—as stated, you can just lean into the combat nature of the Commander, and treat it like a chunky flyer that enjoys tutoring one of a few different Equipment. Being 5 mana really allows you to scale your power based on fast mana, and it's parallel to the fact said fast mana serves as combo pieces. A slower Bounty isn't just slower, it's less consistent in the execution of its best win condition.

Don't be a Moby Dick

Ceran manages to make the whale as majestic & mysterious as it ought to be, helped by smaller versions of the giants flanking our focus.

When I first read this card, I saw it only as a way to break Steelfin Whale and take an Extra Turn, and I was already excited at just that prospect. In really digging into it, however, the H.M.S. Bounty continued to surprise me not only regarding its own flexibility, but the shocking depth of Whales' playability in Magic. In spite of not really being a Creature type you think about often, there's everything here to form a Sisay-style combo engine that fills gaps and solves for awkward gamestates. This is also the first-ever Spacecraft we've covered on Commander Focus, which is a triumph in its own right. I had felt initially that making the card type legal as Commander seemed unmotivated, but after seeing the options from Star Trek it makes quite a bit more sense; that's not to say I'm a fan of all the Spacecraft from the set (why are so many Colorless?) but the good ones are great. I've had a dedicated Spacecraft-matter deck in paper since the release of EOE, in the form of Maester Seymour, but frankly this might unseat it, or at the very least sit alongside it.

That is to say nothing of the fact that we have Nauctis, the Sunken Realm arriving next year, and with it I would assume a whole host of new Whales. We've seen them in promotional art, and given this is a card from the main set, it's perhaps possible Wizards is teeing up some kind of Standard Whale-oriented strategy. I don't take the Bounty as a Standard-playable card, as cool as it is, but I appreciate the potential. While not necessarily as complex as Princess Yue, to whom I always return to when mentioning flavor inadvertently leading to rich mechanical depth, the H.M.S. Bounty is a wildly novel Commander in the grand scheme of things. The type it touches on has had no support prior, and as such may have just become the defacto Knack deck for Blue in Commander. That alone is a huge get, but the fact not one but two combos exist for Whales, on top of a wholly-Whale mana outlet with infinite blinks & mana, is just obscene. It's the kind of thing that makes you wonder if the designers knew this, and moreover, makes you want to build this list in paper. At time of writing, the H.M.S. Bounty has 18 decks on EDHREC, with more sure to come.

Until next time, call me Ishmael.

title: D&D World of Warcraft stars some top-tier new species
content:
Most of the time, Dungeons and Dragons books are pretty sparing about new species. Unless it's a dedicated book like Monsters of the Multiverse, we rarely get more than a handful of new additions to the DnD races list. But D&D World of Warcraft said 'screw that'. It's stuffed with new origin stories, from reflavored Player's Handbook species to brand-new, setting-specific picks. And some of them are actually pretty good.

I'm currently working on a full, thorough review of the new D&D book, which is now available in early access on D&DBeyond. I've already covered the winners and losers of classes. Now, check out the slick DnD races that caught my eye:

Earthen

Earthen are Dwarf-shaped creatures made from living stone. Their history in Azeroth is long and complex, but these crystal-covered, golem-like creatures would be easy to bring into a standard D&D setting. And, for defense-focused characters, it'd be worth it.

Earthen have 120 feet of Darkvision, and they don't gain exhaustion levels from malnutrition. They have resistance to poison damage and advantage on saves against the poisoned condition.

Those are neat tricks, but the main features to get excited about are Quiet Contemplation and Azerite Surge. The first gives you one additional HP per Hit Point Die spent during a short rest.

The second, when you take an attack action on your turn, lets you replace one attack with a 15-foot cone blast that deals 1d10 radiant damage on a failed Dexterity save. The save DC relies on your Constitution modifier and proficiency bonus, and its damage increases at levels five, 11, and 17.

Basically, the Earthen addresses some of the biggest issues with melee builds. That extra pip of HP helps your survivability, and Azerite Surge gives a much-needed attack alternative for foes at range. The species suits Paladins and Barbarians, and other tanky frontliners well.

Goblin

World of Warcraft quietly reprints a few existing species from fifth edition. Spelljammer's Autognome has become a Mechagnome, for example, while Monster of the Multiverse's Goblin didn't even need a name change. Though its rules are neither new nor original, they're still a solid pick for your D&D character, in and out of Azeroth.

Goblins have 60 feet of Darkvision, plus advantage on saves against the charmed condition. More excitingly, Nimble Escape lets them Disengage or Hide as a bonus action - giving other classes a taste of the Rogue's agility.

Another solid ability is Fury of the Small, which deals extra damage equal to your proficiency bonus when you damage a creature at least one size larger than yours. This applies to spells and attacks, so anyone can benefit from the damage boost.

Pandaren

Pandarens appeal thematically, because D&D doesn't currently have an equivalent to 'sentient Panda'. Mechanically, they're enticing too, particularly if you favor melee.

Pandaren have 60 feet of Darkvision and resistance to bludgeoning damage from falling. They also, like our friend the Earthen, regain one extra HP per Hit Point Die spent during a short rest. Lastly comes Quaking Palm. When you hit a creature with a melee attack on your turn, your movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks from the creature you hit until the end of your turn.

This is a slightly tankier, slightly more agile D&D character. Monks are the obvious choice, given Pandaren's lore-accurate lives of discipline and honor. However, a zippy Rogue, Ranger, or Fighter would enjoy that added maneuverability - and who doesn't like extra hit points?

Tauren

Tauren are yak-like humanoids with a historic hatred of centaurs and a tradition tied to druidic magic. These horned, hulking creatures offer martial characters a wide variety of ways to use their attack action.

First, you can use your Horns to perform unarmed strikes, dealing 1d6 + Strength modifier in piercing damage. Many species have an alternate strike like this, and it's rarely meta-destroying. Slightly better is Goring Rush, a feature that lets you make an unarmed strike as a bonus action after taking the Dash action and moving at least 20 feet.

Hammering Horns isn't too shabby either. When you hit a creature with a melee attack action on your turn, you can spend your bonus action to shove a target up to 10 feet away. This species is very reliant on your bonus action, but for certain Fighters and Barbarians, that's a price worth paying.

The main reason to pick this species, however, is Tauren Lineage. Your ancestry gives you one of three additional perks.

First, you could take a blanket +1 AC and resistance to cold damage. Alternatively, when you take the attack action on your turn, you can replace it with a magical stomp. Each creature of your choice within five feet makes a Constitution saving throw, and they're stunned until the end of your turn if they fail. Stunned is a wonderfully powerful condition in D&D, but it only lasting until the end of the current turn limits its value. You could use it to guarantee advantage against nearby foes, or to escape scot-free without opportunity attacks.

Your last lineage option is my favorite. There's an action where you move up to your speed (without triggering opportunity attacks), moving through the spaces of other creatures. Creatures you move through make a Strength save, taking bludgeoning damage equal to your proficiency and Strength modifier, and being knocked prone. Prone is an easily achieved condition thanks to weapon masteries, but this is an extremely entertaining alternative.

Troll

Trolls are the oldest community in Azeroth, and they're a staple of most other fantasy settings. Now a playable D&D species, they're fantastic all-rounders.

Bloodied Frenzy alone is a feature worth chasing. When you're Bloodied, you have guaranteed advantage on all attack rolls. I'm sure somewhere there's an adept character builder who can find a way to keep your Troll stable at slightly less than half health in order to fish for crits.

When you want to heal, you've got the Troll Healing feature, which lets you regain the maximum roll (plus your Constitution modifier) when you spend a Hit Die during a Short Rest.

Running out of Hit Dice? No biggie. Troll Lineage gives you one of three additional benefits, one of which replenishes an expended Hit Die when you use Heroic Inspiration. Alternatively, you can ignore certain difficult terrain types when you Dash (yawn), or you regain a Heroic Inspiration any time you roll a 1 on the D20 (slightly less yawn!).

Trolls also have the customary 60 feet of Darkvision. All of that makes them pretty darned difficult to kill. Once again, frontliners will get most excited about the extra durability, but pretty much any character can benefit.

Vulpera

Vulpera are small, fox-like people (another sentient animal species not currently served by D&D). They have a reputation for cunning and ferocity, which sounds like prime Rogue material. I think a Rogue would enjoy this species' perks, but it's far from limited to a single class or build.

As well as the standard 60 feet of Darkvision, you have resistance to fire damage. Plus, the first time you take damage after you roll Initiative, you reduce the damage taken by your level. That's appealing for the squishier characters in your party.

Additionally, you have Vulpera Nimbleness, which lets you move through the space of any creature a size larger than you. If you can find a way to dodge opportunity attacks (the Swashbuckler subclass, for example), that's a lot of added maneuverability. Huh, maybe this is mainly a Rogue species.

Worgen

Worgens were originally Night Elf druids afflicted by a rage-inducing lupine curse, but they've since learned to deal with their anger issues. Mechanically, this another shape-shifting species, but it's one with a unique set of benefits.

You can change into your bestial form as a bonus action (or for free when you roll Initiative). Doing so gives you temporary HP equal to twice your proficiency bonus, and it lasts for one minute or until you end the effects early. Your speed increases by 10 feet, you have resistance to necrotic damage, and you can move 10 feet as a reaction (without opportunity attacks).

That's several small boosts for an entire combat session, and any of them could be the thing that keeps you alive. This is another strong all-rounder species, though I can see squishy spellcasters getting a lot of use out of that escape hatch reaction.

Want to chat more about Dungeons and Dragons, or keep an eye out for our WoW review? You can stay up-to-date in the official Wargamer Discord.

title: How to Paint Everything: Star Wars Legion - Imperial Stormtroopers and Scout Troopers
content:
Greetings Legionnaires! In today's installment of How to Paint Everything, we are going to be taking a look at how to paint the iconic White Armor that is a staple of Imperial armies across the galaxy. Whether your preferred unit is the Imperial Stormtrooper, Scout Trooper, or Snow Trooper, this article will have you covered.

A huge thank you to Atomic Mass Games for providing the models!

To begin with, similarly to my Rebel Commandos and Rebel Troopers, I had to come up with something that I could paint relatively quickly because I knew I would have to replicate it across several units of models, and didn't want to spend too much time on my basic troopers. Without further ado, let's dive in!

Stormtroopers/ Scout Troopers

Normally, I would say the key to painting White is to not actually paint White. However, in this case, I wanted very few steps, and I wanted high contrast, so I did use white in the recipe.

  1. Like most “white armored” Star Wars troops, I started them with an all-over airbrush of Pro Acryl Bright Warm Grey as a base to build the white upon. I really like this bright shade of grey as a base for any paint job where I am going to have to highlight up to white, or give the illusion of highlighting up to white. It also has really good coverage over my black primer coat.
  2. Next, I gave them a focused highlight of Pro Acryl Bold Titanium White. This is, by far, my favorite white. Usually, the pigments are too big in white paint to work through an airbrush, but somehow Monument has figured out how to make it work. It also has great coverage and is extremely bright, so it can give that great contrast on the armor in just two different colors.  
  3. I painted all of the connecting materials and blaster with Pro Acryl Coal Black. This feels like a pure black paint, but it has a little more depth to it than other black paint I have used before. At this point, they really started to look good enough to put on a table. I did a few selected highlights with Pro Acryl Brown Grey on the connecting material, so it didn’t look like primer. I have used this paint as a base for all of my comic-style non-metallic metals for my Marvel Crisis Protocol minis, so I felt really comfortable using this as a highlight color. It dries much darker than it looks when you apply it, so the highlight is a little bit more subtle than it may initially appear to be when you are putting it on. I absolutely love the little hint of brown in this color, too! It adds so much to the finished paint job! I also chose one color to paint onto the models to help with squad identification. You can really choose whatever color you want for this stage; just keep it consistent for the entire squad.  
  4. At this point, the bulk of the work was done, and it was time to apply a coat of gloss varnish to lock in my progress up until this point. Once I had given the varnish plenty of time to dry, I mixed up odorless spirits and black oil paint to get my usual black oil wash.  If you've never tried this technique before, I highly recommend it.  Because the vast majority of the model was white armor, I really needed this oil wash to do a lot of the heavy lifting when it came to shading the recesses and bringing out the details. It can also give the models a little bit more of a "they've actually been in the field" look than traditional shade washes can (at least in my experience). Then I finished off with a stippled line of Scale75 Black Metal on the blasters so they had a little metallic sheen.
  5. The finishing touches for these models are the same as all of my Legion miniatures. I seal the model with a matte varnish through my airbrush after I paint the black rim around my base. After that, I use Beach Sand, Concrete, and Pacific Blue Water Gel from AK Interactive to build my Scarif-themed bases. After they have had time to dry, I will stipple on some Bold Titanium White across the water to simulate the foam, but I am very tempted to try AK's Water Foam for a more realistic look on my bases. I'll have a tutorial on how to make those bases specifically in another article.

title: "People buy Trench Crusade faster than we can make it" says business lead
content:
"The biggest problem with Trench Crusade is people buy it faster than we can make it and ship it out", says Jamie Parsons, chief operating officer at Factory Fortress Inc. Wargamer's Mollie Russell interviewed Parsons at the huge SPIEL Essen convention, where he was one of the team representing the smash hit skirmish wargame of religious fanatics and grotesquely altered history - here's what he had to say about the studio's meteoric growth.

"From the very beginning, even the first Kickstarter - not the big one that blew up, the one before - it's a project where we only had good problems", Parsons says. Initially joining the team as a Kickstarter project manager, he now handles "all the boring business stuff at Trench Crusade" so the artists can get on with profaning against god and man, making a kick-ass wargame while they do it.

To get a sense for how far Trench Crusade has outstripped the team's expectations, consider the recently released two player box set, Carcass Front. It's a wargaming campaign so scintillating I gave it my first ever 10/10 review, yet Parsons says he was circumspect when deciding how many copies to order.

"For any company that is under two years old in the tabletop industry, if you sell 15,000 of anything, that's great", Parsons says. "So I ordered that many. I was like, if we do this in a year, we'll have made back our investment. We'll be paying our people". The stock sold out in two and a half months.

"We thought we made the correct call", Parsons muses, "we thought we were even being too enthusiastic". The team's only benchmark was the second Kickstarter in 2024, which raked in a staggering $3 million, but Parsons - a veteran of 30 campaigns - was all too aware this was not a reliable indicator. "Some Kickstarter companies see demand, overhire, overequip themselves", he says. "Then when that demand drops, if you mass hire, you must mass fire".

"Now we're starting to actually get sales numbers, so we can see the actual demand - we've been flying blind up till now". The studio has releases planned for most months until March (with a December break), with production lined up with Polish manufacturer Archon Studios. Parsons has a lot of praise for Archon. "We could not pull this off without them. And I say that because some people have been blaming Archon for [our lack of stock] - it is not their problem, it's not their fault, it's just suffering from success".

In fact, Parsons thinks that Archon has been transformational for the industry, simply by making high quality plastic mould production, and high-volume plastic production, feasible in Europe. "Carcass Front took us three months to produce, print plus plastic, and that was 15,000 units of a big product", Parsons says, "If we had to do that in 3D printing, we'd be having this interview next year".

While Factory Fortress Inc is investing heavily into plastic miniature production, Trench Crusade welcomes conversions and fans playing with other models. "If you don't like them, if you don't think they're good enough, we haven't made a good enough product", Parsons says. He's aware "there are other people in certain parts of the world where import [costs mean it's] just not possible to have plastic - I don't want to cut them off". He promises "I'm not going to break into your house and check" - we hope that's a joke.

The big Kickstarter that catapulted Trench Crusade into the limelight came at the end of 2024,  and since completing fulfilment for that Parsons "spent a year getting us out of Kickstarter, transitioning into a serious company, because the two are very different". "One of my objectives was to grow cleverly, so we've been investing in production, especially miniatures", he adds, but "we're very lean in terms of management and actual operations, we need to grow that as well".

But what shape will Factory Fortress and Trench Crusade take? "What makes wargaming so special is it's not just one thing: it's not the miniatures, it's not the painting, it's not the game, it's not meeting people, it's not traveling to go to events or just collecting, it's all of that", Parsons enthuses. Within 10 years, Parsons "would like us to start providing the full shebang, the whole scope", so that "no matter where you are, we've got something for you, and we just want you to enjoy it".

A noble endeavour. Mollie delved deep into Trench Crusade during her time at Essen - check out her interview with lead developer Tuomas Pirinen, the results of the epic Crimson Chalice painting competition, and her experiences as a first time miniature wargamer playing the skirmish game. If you've got a warband you'd like to share, drop some pictures into the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Tabletop Battles’ Eldfall Chronicles Northern Wind Campaign Report, Part II
content:
Welcome back to Sam and Jake's ongoing coverage of Northern Wind, Freecompany's dungeon-crawler board game pitting a ragtag group of misfits against the Oni horde of Mt. Byodo. When last we left our heroes, they had passed the "all your stuff gets stolen" cutscene and tripped the Magic Breaker, restoring their armaments both arcane and mundane. Thusly equipped, they traveled to the Hilltop Temple, the last stop before leaving civilization behind.

Of course, the Oni have gotten here first.

Our heroes arrive seeking shelter and respite, but immediately, something appears wrong: there is nobody to greet them outside the temple, and as they watch, an Oni brute shambles into view. They quickly hide and make a plan: make it over the rickety bridge outside the temple, search for survivors, and push on.

Mission 4 - Hilltop Temple

Sam's Mission

Because Na'ra and Anari fully cleared the Profane Burners (and I therefore have Purple Fate C), Na'ra gets the chance to do a Ghost Sniff (an INT role at -3) which she heroically passes - meaning that I spot the undead right away, rather than having to stumble into them. There are two Vengeful Spirits in front of me, and then a Forgotten Hero (an archer samurai skeleton) on the bridge.

But the whole party is together now, so there's nothing to worry about. Tharos goes first, shooting a spirit. The crossbow bolt passes right through, but that's a Weak Point inflicted. Reacting, both Spirits drift into the square where Seigen and Na'ra are waiting for them. Seigen gets to show off his Sweep attack - he hits both spirits, shrugs off their counterswing, and poofs one into nonexistence. Na'ra makes short work of the second.

The archer might be a problem. The bridge he's on is too narrow for our party, and we'll have to go single file. Anari prepares by enchanting Tharos's bow with flame, and Tharos darts out to the end of the bridge, taking a potshot at Mr. Skellington. He inflicts a weak point, but the skeleton archer's aim is true, and his Reactive shot hits Tharos (possibly in the knee) and Incapacitates him. Luckily, Tharos was carrying one of my three Medicines and will be getting up soon, but I was hoping those would last a little longer.

Anari deploys her ice spikes and hits the skeleton, inflicting another Weak Point, but that's it. It's time for the hostiles' active turn, which means that we're flipping a Chaos Deck card for the first time!

The result: nasty weather. A blizzard, in fact, which makes the whole board Dense and Hazy. This radically cuts down on the effectiveness of ranged attacks... which is actually good news, because that skeleton prefers to use his bow if at all possible, and his turn is utterly ineffective due to the flying snow. Our heroes' ranged reactions are as well, but on our next turn, Na'ra bounds up and, you guessed it, shoves his bony ass right off the bridge. Splat!

With the enemies dealt with, it's time to explore. Our heroes have noticed a small ledge down below the bridge; perhaps, if they had a [Climbing Rope], they could make it down there! However, it's not all good news: there's another slightly beaten-up Oni Marauder, though this one has some loot.

Fortunately, the gruesome foursome has enough time to plan their attack, and Seigen stands one tile ahead of everyone else, shielding them with his body. I'm able to lard up the Oni with Weak Points (and a Wound) before he can act, so when his turn comes around, Seigen can React with a melee attack, forcing a Confrontation that Seigen automatically wins with a Critical Hit by cashing in Weak Points. Score! The party makes short work of biggun and goes through his pockets.

Surprise! It's rope.

Na'ra. Credit: keewa

Na'ra takes it and goes to find out what's on the ledge, while the rest of us approach the temple courtyard. Turns out it's occupied: there's a full-strength Oni Marauder (a Lieutenant, in fact - a Boss Monster modification that, at least in my edition, appears to have no mechanical effect) and he's guarding the gate to the temple. When he spots us, he smashes the gate controls, and the heavy portcullis starts to descend.

Tharos darts forward and manages to stop the gate from crashing, but that's all he can do - if he moves or takes any other action, it will fall. Chuckling, the Oni lumbers forward, and we notice some poor, tied-up prisoners in the yard.

I'm also told to place a Dire Ambush Chaos card into the deck, fourth from the top. I am not looking forward to what happens when it flips.

When the next hostile turn comes around, the Chaos Deck flips another Weather condition: Sleet. Strangely, this actually cancels both weather conditions, meaning that, effectively, nothing happens. Stranger still, this requires me to shuffle the cards into the deck - so now the Dire Ambush could be anywhere.

The sudden clear skies are not good news for Tharos, who is now stuck in plain sight. The Oni walks right up to him and swings that huge club, and Tharos decides discretion is the better part of valor; he Dodges backwards, luckily escaping a richly deserved squashing, but that means the gate falls the rest of the way and blocks the path. Great.

Na'ra, a skilled climber, uses the rope to climb down to the ledge, and finds that she can climb up the far side into the courtyard. This she does, while my other heroes try to bash open the gate, and the Oni... sort of taunts them from the far side? It's a little odd, to be honest, him just standing here. He doesn't even notice Na'ra sneaking into the courtyard behind him; the way Oni Marauders' Reactive turns are described, he won't react at all to her as long as she doesn't get too close.

Na'ra manages to free some prisoners, including Asano (again), and finds some loot: another dagger, a lantern, and some Precious Materials, which can be used later on to activate some advanced synergy powers. The rest of the party is having a tougher time of it: the gate has five hit points and armor 8, which means that, even enhanced by Anari's sorcery, Seigen struggles to scratch it. The whole party unloads into the gate with no effect at all. Meanwhile, on the Hostile Turn, the Oni notices Na'ra and goes chasing after her - but a truly heroic series of Dodge reactions keeps her unscathed, as she flips and darts away from him one tile at a time.

The rest of the party decides "fuck this" and hurries over to the ledge. Without Na'ra's climbing ability, getting them down the rope is painfully slow; you can't take any action if you Climb as a special movement, so you're limited to your base movement, without even a Dodge for an extra square. Worse, as they're shimmying like the world's least impressive gym class, that Dire Ambush shows up, spawning in an Oni Marauder and a Red Yaksha (another big, scary Oni).

This is genuinely bad. Those two are beelining for the gate, are poised to smash it to splinters, will then join their boss, and our heroes can't escape if there are any hostiles in the courtyard. Luckily, Na'ra has been continuing her hot Dodge streak, and now the party is all united. The Oni, seeing a cluster of enemies, decides to Hulk Smash the team, but Seigen's Fencing ability reduces him to one swing. Seigen and the Oni match swings in their Confrontation role, but while Seigen wounds the Oni, the big boy fails to crack Seigen's armor or Anari's, which is actually kind of impressive. Tharos, meanwhile, dodges nimbly away. From there, it's pretty much over; I have four heroes' worth of magic and weaponry, and the big boy goes down just as his friends start hacking at the fallen gate. Before they can get through, we're through the temple door and away, pausing only so Asano can hand us his special heirloom cloak.

Asano's Magic Puffer Jacket is actually pretty cool - I'm going to give it to Seigen. It makes him resistant to Profane enemies, which I imagine I'll be seeing a lot of. I have to play a little bit of inventory juggling at this point, with all the crap I've looted, but it turns out not to be a problem. Tharos is apparently yoked as hell, and his 10-item storage capacity easily encompasses all of the various sharp and shiny things we've scrounged so far. Plus, his hawk came back. Remember he had a hawk?

I have some Weak Points - Tharos, Anari and Seigen each took one - and that's not great. They persist between missions, so I'll have to figure out if there's some way to get rid of them before I meet an enemy that can use them.

Jake's Mission

Reading through Sam's experience, I was struck with how different things can play out even though we're playing the same mission with the same characters. In fact, there aren't very many possible ways for our paths to have branched at this point and yet our finales played out quite differently. Neat!

This mission is also continuing the trend of these tutorial missions where game mechanics are gradually added. It's a great way to introduce players to what's honestly quite a lot of moving parts, but since it's broken up it doesn't feel overwhelming. This time around we're adding in the Chaos Deck. The Chaos Deck is a fixed list of cards for each mission -- we'll be gradually adding and removing cards from it as the story continues, shaping it into a unique set of threats and surprise situations throughout the gameplay. For the most part, they're bad things. You already got a taste of some of the nasty ambushes possible, along with various weather events and other unpleasant things that can happen to our heroes.

Speaking of weather, now that the Chaos Deck is in play, we start each mission by flipping the top three cards of the deck. If any of them are weather cards, we start the game with that weather effect in play. Considering this story takes place while our brave heroes are scaling a frigid mountain covered in snow, a lot of these weather events are going to play into that.

One similarity in my game with Sam's is that my Na'ra also was able to pass her INT check in order to trigger the first encounter immediately. This was great because the Vengeful Spirits would otherwise have spawned in between my party members and it doesn't take a tactical genius to realize that wouldn't be ideal.

I took a careful look at the Vengeful Spirits' behavior card to see what exactly they would do. It turns out that as long as you aren't within melee range and aren't attacking them, they're content to not react at all and will just float there menacingly. I feel like carefully managing these behaviors is going to be super important as even more threatening monsters enter the fray. Seeing my opportunity here, I chose to have Anari activate first to enchant Seigen's sword with Burning Touch which would let him ignore the annoying Incorporeal ability the ghosts have. My beefy Ranger from the Empire of Soga went next by stepping into the space with the spirits and simply chopping though both of them with his flaming two-handed sword. That was easy.

Easy aside from the fact that Anari caught a reactive shot from the Forgotten Hero in her face, that is. She immediately dropped after enchanting Seigen. This is starting a long trend of Anari being a problematic party member for me.

The Forgotten Hero wasn't much of a problem after this point because it had spent both of its action points firing at Anari (successfully) and Seigen (unsuccessfully). Na'ra moved up and used some totally okay profane necromancy magic to heal Anari before rushing forward some more. The Mau can really move. Once back on her feet, the Helian threw out a barrage of Ice Spikes (a STK 3 ranged spell is so good) and was accompanied by two shots from Tharos' fancy crossbow to make it class dismissed for Doctor Skelebones.

Why did I rush forward? I kind of forgot but I think the idea was I wanted to trigger the encounter as soon as possible to get it over with. No, that doesn't make much sense in hindsight. Regardless, the injured Oni Marauder (with convenient rope) pops up, beats up my heroes, and eventually goes down. I have to use Medicine to bring Na'ra back to her feet and a Healing Potion on Seigen to top him off as well, but after that point I have the secret path unlocked. I trigger the "cutscene" that causes the gate to fall, but I decide not to bother trying to catch it and just let the thing drop closed. The Oni Raidleader gets pissed, but all my heroes just book it away and down through the secret passage to pop up behind him.

Fortunately, Na'ra and Tharos both have the Climb skill, so they're able to navigate down to the ledge and back up into the Temple Courtyard without slowing down. Seigen and Anari follow along at a slower pace both because they have to spend an entire activation to climb and because they're both only moving two spaces instead of the Rin who can move 3.

All four of my heroes make it into the courtyard and start beating on the Oni Raidleader. He doesn't go down without a fight -- the short version is that I burn through all of my remaining healing items before striking the killing blow. They do all manage to take out the Raidleader, tend their wounds, and free the prisoners before the Dire Ambush card is revealed and after reading Sam's experience I am pretty grateful for it. Seigen gets his fancy Warding Pelt but also walks out with a weak point and a wound. Na'ra is sporting a weak point herself. Surely this won't be a problem in the next mission.

Closing Thoughts

Sam: This mission is quite a bit more complex than the prior three, with a real "let's put it all together" vibe. That said, there were a few moments here that made me scratch my head. Some are likely just copyediting errors (is the Oni by the exit a Lieutenant or a Raidleader? And is there supposed to be some mechanical modification from his status, whatever it is? Just using the Raidleader card?), but others feel a little baffling. The Dire Ambush - is the intent really that you shuffle the deck when you draw a second Weather event (not that rare an occurrence, given the limited size of the deck)? Is the gate supposed to be that tough to crack through? I ended up using the ledge for everyone, because I could tell it was going to take forever to hack down the gate. And what about Climb - how does that work? The way I played it, my characters can, on their activation, take a normal move and treat the rope as a one-tile step, but they can't do any actions if that's what they choose to do with their turn.

What is the Lieutenant/Raidleader supposed to do when the gate drops with him on the other side from the party? Just stare at them through the bars? Is the party really supposed to be able to handle a Red Yaksha and two Marauders at once if you're too slow in clearing the gate/killing the boss? It felt at times a little loose, like things weren't quite coming together in the way the developers intended.

Overall, though, it was fun to be put through a bit more of a high-stakes challenge. Now the Moon Dial, which tracks the time we've spent, and the Event deck come into play.

Jake: The Oni Raidleader was a showcase in how the threat level of a monster can jump up with just a few tweaks, namely having a higher STA value which results in more action points each turn. In fact, aside from having two additional hit points those are the only changes between this boss and a vanilla Oni Marauder, but it was felt. I guess the unit card also has spooky glowing eyes which is a nice touch.

As for Sam's question on climb, I did have to look this one up while playing because I missed it in the first go-through of the book.

The way an activation works is that you spend the activation token, then the character declares a Normal Movement or Special Movement. After declaring it, the model is moved. Following the movement step, the model declares a Normal Action or Special Action. Essentially, you can combine a Normal Movement and Normal Action or pick a Special Movement or pick a Special Action. That's not exactly how it works out, but it's close enough to get the point across.

There are only two Normal Movement options -- one is to walk (move equal to the model's speed) and the other is to idle (only rotate but otherwise remain stationary, but this is the only way to do a Special Action). The Special Movement options are Run (move twice the model's speed), Climb (move the model's speed over elevated ground), or Jump (move the model's speed across a space). If a model has the Climbing skill like Tharos or Na'ra do, they can do a Climb Special Movement as a Normal Movement, allowing them to follow it up with any other Normal Action like an attack or dodge.

Mission 5 - Byodo Summit Gateway

Sam's Mission

Here we are - the last stop before we begin our climb. The Summit Gateway is the final crossroads before the "true ascent begins," and divides the path in three: westward through Mt. Akashi, eastward through Mt. Senjo, or straight ahead, through the Shivering Valley of Shimodani.

On the way, I draw my first two event cards, and of course it's nothing good; Ill Omens distributes four Weak Points among my heroes (leaving Na'ra with one and everyone else with two), and Anari is wracked with Night Terrors that leave her at -2 to all stats this mission. At least she can still hand out buffs. I select Bolstered Prowess as the Synergy I'm trying to achieve this mission. As a refresher, Synergy cards start out locked, and have an unlock condition. Every time you achieve it, you get a Synergy point, and when you reach the target number of points the Synergy unlocks as a permanent buff to one of your characters. This one scores when an Enchanted hero incapacitates an enemy, and requires two points to unlock - and I have a Precious Materials to give it a free point. Once unlocked, the hero who unlocked it gets +3 OFF and DEF for as long as they're enchanted. Not bad on Seigen!

The Gateway path is deceptively simple: a straight road, with branches on each side. One has an Oni Marauder, the other a Forgotten Hero, but they're both facing away from me and Distracted. Per the mission rule, they still Distracted until one of them can see us, but they're positioned 3 tiles away from the path forward, and a Crouched hero isn't in LOS outside of 3 spaces away. I could in theory sneak past them in a crouch, but I'd rather not leave them alive as I pass by.

I hand out some enchantments: Tharos gets Anari's Burning Touch, while Seigen gets Na'ra's Necrotic Wound. My party aim for the Forgotten Hero first, and Tharos manages to snipe him in the back of the head with a Burning crossbow bolt. Burn means that when you inflict a wound, you get to roll damage again, at 0 armor this time, and potentially deal a second wound - thus, Tharos blows the hero's head smoove off without it even getting to un-Distract.

I'm not totally sure about how this works, but I don't think that the Marauder is un-Distracted by this either, since the Hero never turned around to draw LoS to me. So I sneak over to get ready to pounce on him, too. The turn flips over to the Hostiles, which means we flip a Chaos Card, and a freezing wind blows in. This is a pretty brutal event; all characters have to test Toughness at the start of each turn (though they can add their armor as a modification) or become Fatigued, which effectively costs them their turn - and if they have any wounds on them, they might take another. But the Hostile Oni doesn't have LOS to my lurking team, and just stands there shivering.

On my turn, things start to go right. My heroes all pass their toughness checks against the cold and move in on the Oni, fully enchanted and ready to take care of business. This happens in fairly short order; Tharos peppers him with bolts, letting the Oni waste both of his reactive AP dodging towards him, and Na'ra and Seigen move in to finish him off. Seigen deals the finishing blow while enchanted with Anari's Burning Touch, activating my Synergy ability.

For the moment, there's no hostiles on the field; it's unclear whether we still have to have a Hostile Turn, so I do out of an abundance of caution. Nobody fails their toughness check again, though it's close for poor Anari, who isn't dressed for this. The Chaos Deck spews forth a tier 1 enemy - one of those dinky little spirits, which Anari trivially banishes with ice shards as a Reaction. On my turn, though, the cold is a little too much for poor Na'ra, who really isn't dressed for this. The others advance, spawning another Oni Marauder guarding the gateway to the exit room and causing some treasure to appear in the room itself.

Again, we go hard into this Oni, even with Na'ra out of commission. Anari peppers him with ice shards, slowing him and damaging him, and Tharos and Seigen finish him off before he can take a turn. Even better, the next Chaos card is weather as well, which cancels the freezing wind and leaves the battlefield clear.

We're on fire! Nothing can go wrong! This is not foreshadowing!

Our heroes start off by looting the courtyard, uncovering a Magatama (which gives the bearer - currently Tharos - an extra wound) and a Weaver's War Scepter, which, once I trade it to Anari, will give her magic attacks a boost. Seigen walks up to the exit, which has the last encounter tile on it... and here comes Guren, the Red Rasetsu.

Remember how I mentioned Demonic Sexual Dimorphism in my original Northern Wind review? Guren is a classic example; I would describe her look as "fanservice-y Karlach," but her stat card makes my eyes water. Three Stamina, ten wounds, Berserker 3 to shrug damage and give her a nasty combat art, Duelist to cancel enemy combat arts, Cleave to do two wounds for each one that goes through, and she can exploit my Weak Points to give herself Unstoppable, meaning you can't cancel her hits in Confrontation (though she can't cancel yours either, the way it's worded).

Guren, the Red Rasetsu. Credit: keewa

Still, the mission ends if I can drop her HP below 4, so I only have to do 7 damage. That's... doable, right? Right? We'll see.

Seigen's first up. He hacks at her, and my dice are pretty hot; her first counterattack misses entirely, and that cost her one of the WP on Seigen. I carve into her for a couple of damage, inflicting Bleed as well. My second attack isn't as lucky - I deal an additional point of damage, as well as a Weak Point from an attack that hits but doesn't penetrate, but she spends her second WP and gets a hit in on me as well. That one hit cleaves Seigen for two damage (but fortunately not Crippling or Panicking him, as he passes his Toughness test and is Fearless).

Na'ra moves in and claws at Guren, inflicting a fourth wound and the Weakened and Poisoned states from her Necrotic Wound-boosted attack. I imagine she has some extremely annoying neko-chan battle cry - "Meow! Take that!" - but the counterswing puts Na'ra down and, with Sweep, takes out Seigen's last wound as well. So both of my my melee hitters are down for the count. Tharos takes a shot, risking the shooting into melee penalty, but fails to penetrate Guren's armor. At least she gets a Weak Point.

Fortunately, Na'ra has medicine, and stands up in the next Strategic phase. For once I draw a positive Chaos card, which would let me heal wounds by cashing in AP, although the only character with missing wounds is Seigen and he's Incapacitated (and therefore has no AP).

The enraged Guren doesn't take any damage from Bleed or Poison, and loses the Weakened and Poisoned states. She's hopping mad now and going after Na'ra. Fortunately, Na'ra has a couple of dodges available; unfortunately, "a couple" is fewer than "three," and Guren is too accurate to simply hope she misses. On the third swing, Na'ra is out of gas, and she goes down.

Thanks to the dodging, though, Guren is now out of melee range, and so Anari and Tharos both React and hit her with ranged attacks, putting her fifth Wound and third Weak Point on her. She still doesn't take any Bleed damage, but now it's my turn; Tharos backs off and shoots her twice, and with Assassinate, he's able to knock the last couple of wounds off of her.

Whew!

With the Rasetsu out of the way, we are approached by a Guildsworn Knight, our second DMPC of the adventure. He is nonplussed at the fact that the gigantic army he expected has been reduced to four people, but seems to believe that we can still pull it off, which is frankly not a thrilling conclusion for me; it certainly suggests that either he's delusional about our chances now, or the planning stage of this mission misread the required force by several orders of magnitude. But, you know, we soldier on, stiff upper lip and all that, lions led by... do they have donkeys in Calad? Or lions, for that matter?

We're fully healed by DM fiat the Guildsworn Knight's totally rad first aid skills, and we all level up to Level 2. Critically, this means Na'ra and Tharos pick up their second Wound (and Anari can carry the Magatama and get her second that way). Anari gets Level 3 Cryomancy and Level 2 Enchanting, giving me some really potent new spells. And everyone picks up some additional stats scattered about, which is welcome.

The Knight tells us that we can take the Western route and face Guren again - that route has fewer, but stronger enemies. Or we could go East and face a blue Rasetsu, a prospect which does not thrill me much. Or we could go straight ahead through the Shivering Valley, but since both the in-game text and the italicized warnings in the campaign book both say that's not an option for beginners, I think I'll pass. We're heading West; if muscle mommy Guren wants to step on me again, well, that's a Woman's Prerogative.

Jake's Mission

Here's everything all set up before the heroes take their first turn. I've picked up a Gamegenic token organizer which comes in handy given the massive number of tokens that this game comes with. Also pictured is a Costco croissant. Yum.

I thought it'd be nice to get a little snapshot of where my heroes were all at when coming into this final tutorial mission. I've actually burned through all of the consumable items by this point; I'm making a point to not hoard items which is my tendency in most games. I don't want to end this game with a chest full of untouched healing potions!

Na'ra has a weak point and her trusty claws, along with a buckler and dagger she has picked up. Between the extra +1 STK on her claws when going after an enemy without action points and her ability to buff herself for free in the strategic phase, this squishy necromancer winds up being a potent melee threat. The buckler is a tiny boost to her otherwise incredibly lackluster durability.

Anari hasn't picked up much in the way of items. Her arcane monocle continues to provide the Foresight effect which doesn't seem particularly useful to me yet. The shortsword and dagger pairing are really just there because she had room and I had the items kicking around. If she ever has to swing one, we're in trouble but at least this way she can engage enemies.

Tharos (and Batu) continue to make good use of that early Thenian crossbow, allowing him to strike with an accurate 16 or less on a d20 and wound on a 19 or less (before factoring in enemy armor) thanks to his Assassination I combat arts. He's also carrying two backup weapons in the dagger and hatchet, both of which can be thrown to take advantage of his decent ACC.

Seigen is bringing over a wound and a weak point into this mission, but he's also the most decked out. His recently acquired warding pelt will help against any spells or profane attacks. The Stonesplitter Nagamaki and shortsword give him two different options for close combat -- the latter is helpful if he's sharing a space with allies because I don't want to catch Na'ra in the sweep of the massive two handed sword. He's also equipped with a rope which means three of my four party members have Climbing. The lantern is just hanging out in case it's useful at some point and I figured if anyone was going to carry it, it'd be the big man himself.

I find it amusing that after digging through the entire pile of Synergy cards, I wound up picking the same Bolstered Prowess to work on that Sam did. Getting +3 OFF/DEF felt like such a huge upgrade, especially considering Anari is an enchanter and can thus cast these buffs without having to roll. There were a few others I was between, but the fact that I thought I could reliably unlock this in a session is what tipped me over the edge to taking it.

Unlike Sam, I decided to try the stealthy approach to getting through this mission. Knowing that enemies can only see crouched heroes if they're within three tiles of them meant there was a safe space in the central tile of the four-way junction. Each hostile round, the enemies had a special behavior to turn 180 degrees, meaning that even if you couldn't get out of the way, a hero could safely stay crouched there (like Anari is doing in this example).

A very important thing is that all the black tile edges count as solid walls, so they're blocking line of sight. The white edges, however, are not line of sight blocking and it means enemies can see across them. Yes, this is a problem considering I left the Forgotten Hero standing there with a clear line of sight into the final room. We'll get there eventually.

In the meantime, I felt pretty clever for bypassing two enemies and triggered the next encounter. This spawned the second Oni Marauder seen above but also two Superior Loot tokens in the final room. After a brief glance at the loot table, there are some really juicy options there so I 100% planned to snag both of those before the final fight. They were even conveniently placed ahead of the final encounter trigger marker which surely isn't just bait for a greedy idiot like myself.

Na'ra and Seigen make quick work of the Oni Marauder. They used to seem far more threatening, but learning to stack buffs and bait out the reactions has meant I can fairly reliably take one out from full health. This time it was a mix of ranged attacks from Anari and Tharos to burn away the Oni's AP, then Seigen and Na'ra beat the crap out of it. It was over-killed by a wound and was poisoned when it went down which is pretty rad.

Patting myself on the back, I moved into the final room and this is where I realized I had a bit of a problem. I couldn't make it to the two loot tokens without being in line of sight of the Forgotten Hero. That skeleton has a pretty wicked ranged attack that not only can do some ranged stabbing, but it also threatens to poison my heroes for further damage and has Stagger which drains their action points.

I was trying to figure out how I wanted to handle this when I passed over to the enemy turn. So far I haven't called out any of the Chaos cards because they haven't been super impactful, but this time I flipped Terror's Embrace which prompted a party-wide morale test. Seigen is fearless, Tharos and Na'ra passed with flying colors, but Anari...

Anari fled away from the surviving Oni Marauder and went straight into line of sight for the Forgotten Hero. He peppered her with arrows and down she went. On my turn, I had Na'ra bring Anari back up with some necromantic flavored healing before failing an attempt at buffing Tharos's ranged attacks. Since Anari was incapacitated at the start of my turn, she didn't gain any action points and thus couldn't buff Tharos either. Tharos was only able to get a single point of damage off but I positioned him so he could react to the Forgotten Hero's upcoming attacks and hopefully finish the undead off.

Fortunately, that's exactly what happened in the following hostile turn. The skeleton shot Tharos, Tharos shot back in response, and the Rin managed to win the confrontation to take out the skeleton. Hooray. The initial Oni Marauder continued to spin around in circles because he had no idea where we were.

Feeling fairly good about my positioning, I started the hero turn with Na'ra giving herself Necrotic Wound per usual thanks to her Artificer class (this granted her Cleave, basically doubling her damage and Poison II, poisoning the target and forcing them to take a penalized save or take more damage). Anari lit Seigen's sword on fire again and then I ran Seigen into the final encounter token which caused the terrifying Red Rasetsu, Guren, to join the fray. Holy shit, she's scary.

That said, I got darn close to one-rounding her. Between a few pot-shots from Anari and Tharos (causing Guren to dodge back and forth between the two), Seigen's flaming sword, and a juiced up Na'ra with her Necrotic Wound enchanted claws, I was able to push through six damage and poison onto Guren. This was after she shrugged off two damage due to her Berserker class benefit, too. All I needed was to pass the turn and have her roll a 10 or higher on a T check at the start of the monster turn and she's go down before getting to activate.

Yeah, she rolled a 7 and the pain train was coming to town. For her first attack, she swung into Seigen. Guren is the first encounter where the enemy can exploit weak points on the characters. When she does so, she does the normal thing of turning a hit into a crit but it also applies the Unstoppable trait to her attack. This means no matter what the results are of a confrontation, successful rolls do not block and anything rolling low enough to hit will go through for both parties. In what is probably the most cinematic ending possible, Seigen and Guren managed to stab each other. Seigen's damage went through, bringing Guren down to below the threshold to trigger the cutscene. Seigen had a large, desecrated relic blade shaped hole in him but he was still (unsteadily) on his feet meaning none of my heroes went down during this insane fight.

The two superior loot tokens gave my heroes some pretty nice swag. One was an accessory that allows a failed AG roll to be rerolled. I imagine this will be a second chance on a dodge 99% of the time. Continuing the defensive trend, I picked up a healing potion and some modified light protection to further boost the ARM of one of my characters. I haven't fully decided where these will all end up, but I'm currently leaning toward giving Na'ra one of them and Anari the other.

The secret log that I read after removing enough wounds from Guren is that she's pretty insane and thought this was a lot of fun. However, her boss recalled her so we'll probably meet again in the future. A Guildsworn Knight meets up with the battered party, tends to their wounds (which also lets the party level up!), and lets the party know the three options available to them. Mount Akashi is where Guren hangs out and it says Marauders are common. Mount Senjo has "countless undead" lead by the Blue Rasetsu. Shimodani, the Shivering Valley, is more of a mystery. It has unpredictable weather, is governed by "???" and has a warning that it isn't for inexperienced players.

I haven't decided where to go yet. Given that Sam is taking the Mount Akashi path, I'm tempted to try one of the others just so we can get some more variety. On the other hand, it could be cool to see how two playthroughs of the same path could diverge. If anyone has suggestions, I'm all ears!

Final Thoughts

Sam: My playthrough of this missions really hammered home just how swingy this ruleset can be. I went through the first three bad guys like prune juice through a short grandmother thanks to (not very many) lucky rolls; Guren nearly took out my whole party thanks to even fewer good rolls on her end. I thought this was a "supposed to lose" fight and, frankly, I wouldn't be surprised if more than half of the people who try this scenario do lose it, especially if they're less cautious than me. That said, losing still progresses the campaign, so it's really more of a cinematic to introduce you to one of the big villainesses of the setting.

What I'm really seeing here is that a key strategy going forward will be to attack a big Hostile to draw out their AP making useless Reactions (many hostiles, when attacked from range, will merely Dodge closer to the attacker), then, when they're out of AP, blitz them down; Seigen and Anari have three-hit attacks, and even Tharos can force two damage rolls if you enchant him with Burn. It's an effective strategy; not without risks, but it's safer than getting into Confrontations with Oni. But we'll see how long it works.

Jake: I feel like I had substantially better luck in this mission than any of the previous ones. I was able to alpha strike most of the threatening enemies with overwhelming force before they were able to cause too much harm to the party. Part of it was some hot dice, but I'd like to think I'm also maybe getting a little better? Time will tell.

I definitely agree with Sam about an effective tactic being action point baiting. It makes me want to pick up some dinky ranged weapon for Seigen to be able to use even if it won't be threatening much damage -- simply making an attack from far away can be monumentally important. I'm not sure how much sway we have over what loot shows up, but it's something I'll be on the lookout for.

I also need to remember enchantments can go on Tharos, because I really like the sound of Burning Touch (or the armor ignoring Melting Touch now that Anari has leveled up!) going onto his crossbow.

For anyone who's been following along, are there any preferences on which route I take? Tell me in the comments or in the Tabletop Battles Discord server!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
